articles.title: Tarek Atoui’s Turbine Hall review – hallelujah, it’s raining musical instruments!
articles.text:
On the floor of the Turbine Hall, there are wide water basins and huge flattish rough-hewn rocks you might see on moorland or in a desert. You can sit or stand or climb on them. But if you look up, you won’t be able to stop looking up – because it’s raining musical instruments. Immense elongated brass trumpets and giant glowing drums seem to float in the air, suspended from the girders of the former power station’s roof.

If Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui had just left it at that, it would be an impressive, intriguing installation, but this is Tate Modern, honey, and Atoui hasn’t been asked to occupy its grandest space with mere physical objects. Instead, his sculptural creations and found stuff resonate and echo with an ever-changing, invisible art of noises. An earth-shaking bass note throbs from a hanging trumpet – or is it from that translucent cone rising out of the ground like an ethereal minaret? Then a drumbeat booms through the space and a woman’s plangent, achingly lovely voice sings notes of infinite nostalgia and melancholy.

It’s entrancing. The music has you hooked. It is music, I think, though abstract, non-melodic, a rising and falling of sounds that lead you around and through the installation’s forest of solid things. But then – is music ever not sculptural? Listening to the scything percussive notes of Stravinsky certainly is; and the desire to crystallise sound waves into something visible has haunted everyone from the inventors of opera to designers of psychedelic lightshows.

Yet Tarek Atoui still manages to do something new and beautiful with sound and vision. He teases you and boggles your mind with how his musical instruments relate to the sounds you hear, how the stones and water basins, pipes and strings have produced this sonic outpouring. The entire installation is an interconnected musical machine.

It’s funny too. There’s a warm, generous if absurdist humour to it all. In the past, a crazy mechanical contraption like this would be called “Heath Robinsonish”, after the early 20th-century British cartoonist who came up with such things. A better comparison is Leonardo da Vinci, who invented wild musical instruments among his other real and impossible machines: organs worked by water, a string instrument shaped like a fantastic beast.

Atoui, like Leonardo, seems to be looking for a lost harmony in the world, a secret note that pleased the Lord. Sadness hovers in the sounds that fill this vast grey space, as the bass notes pound harder, building up to an apocalyptic blast. What is being mourned and where is he taking us? You start to feel you are in a city of sounds and sights. The crowd of towering, floating pinnacles, the mysterious voice and crescendo of percussion, suggest an ancient, tumultuous labyrinth of a city. I thought of Lahore and Marrakesh, of a street-singer heard once in an Istanbul market. Yet this city is purer, less tangible. Its towers fly in the air.

Ultimately, you can’t reduce this magical, elusive work of art to a fixed meaning. You have to surrender to it. The sound gathers you up in its ecstasy like a spiralling mystical dance. There is a strong similarity with Sufi drummers and dervishes who use music and motion to inculcate a liberating, trancelike calm. I certainly didn’t want to leave. The vibrations and complex visual composition keep your brain busy but you are also soothed and at peace.

It also suggests the urban life all around this site, the exotic sounds of Bankside: the music of the city, gathered into Atoui’s collage of random noise. But reality slips and fades as you are shown a world beyond the physical. All these objects, from the cones to the stones to the electric guitar played live at the press view, are but as air. They fascinate the eye but the sound eventually dissolves the material world. The solid stuff Atoui begins with becomes as unreal as a reflection in a courtyard pool.

Atoui has grabbed the opportunity to work in this vast space with both hands, creating something rich, ingenious, funny, sad, mystical. This is a Turbine Hall installation to lose yourself in for hours, dreaming and wondering. It’s the sonic answer to a sun indoors – and Atoui is a modern magus.

articles.title: ‘When it went double platinum, Andy Burnham gave us the award’: how Courteeners made Not Nineteen Forever
articles.text:
Liam Fray, songwriter/vocals, guitar

I had the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever before the band existed. They were in a little red book of poems and scribbles that got me a place on the creative writing course at the University of Salford. Most of what became the songs for our first album, St Jude, were in that book. As well as uni, I was working in a shop and spending five nights a week at the Night & Day bar in Manchester, but in a nightclub I’d be the dude scribbling in the corner while everyone else was dancing or copping off.

Not Nineteen Forever was probably inspired by a specific incident, although I can’t remember it exactly. The first line, “She had to peel me off the pavement”, could have happened on many a night out then. “Front-crawled the crowd down the stairs” is because the staircase at the 42nd Street club was so tight you’d have to literally front-crawl over people. The chorus: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together”, sounds like the sort of thing somebody might have said to me, but it could easily have been me giving myself a telling off after waking up with a fuzzy head.

I got the chords when I was trying to work out Someday by the Strokes but got the finger positions muddled up. I’d taken a bag of washing to my parents’ house and was working on it in my old bedroom when my dad poked his head in and said: “It sounds all right, that.” Not Nineteen Forever was one of the last songs I wrote before I convinced my three best mates to form the band. I told them: “If you don’t do this with me, I’ll be playing acoustic guitar on my own in Manchester pubs for ever.”

You never think a song’s going to resonate 20 years later, but it’s become easily Courteeners’ most popular song. Ironically, it initially charted at No 19, but years later when it went double platinum Andy Burnham – who comes to our gigs – presented us with the award in the Britons Protection pub. The song’s taken on a poignant dimension now. At gigs I see our original fans together with their kids – who are 17, 18, 19 – and they’re all singing: “You’re not nineteen forever, pull yourself together.”

Stephen Street, producer

Courteeners had just been signed by a major label who asked me if I could go to Manchester to meet them as they had expressed interest in working with me. I saw them play in one of the university halls and it was mind-blowing. They already had a devoted following who were singing along with the lyrics the way Smiths audiences used to. I’d produced the Smiths, so it was right up my avenue.

In the mid-2000s there’d been a resurgence of indie guitar bands: Arctic Monkeys, Kaiser Chiefs and Kasabian. In a way Courteeners were the last hurrah of that kind of hugely popular guitar group. The next thing I knew we were all in Olympic studios in London recording the album. I was excited to work with them. Not Nineteen Forever was a ready-made anthem and stood out, but so did Cavorting or What Took You So Long?

With a band like Courteeners, you want to capture their performance. Like the best bands, they were like a little gang: us against the world. So we recorded live, only using click tracks to set the tempos. Their arrangements were short and concise and didn’t need much editing. Liam and Conan [Daniel Moores]’s guitar parts were intrinsic to the sound – I lent Conan a nice old vintage Telecaster – and I found the emotion in Liam’s voice really attractive.

When they’d started out in a garage, Liam had to shout to be heard over the guitar, but in the studio I vaguely remember telling him he didn’t need to. When I saw the lyrics to Not Nineteen Forever written down it hit me how good they were. “Older woman and an ever so slightly younger man” always makes me laugh. He was 19. The “older woman” was probably 21 or something.

When the album came out I was perplexed by the lukewarm reaction from elements of the press – probably because it was another four lads with guitars – but it’s a really strong collection that I think still stands up today. The reissue of St Jude went to No 1 15 years after it first came out. I’d never had that happen before in my career: I was quite emotional.

articles.title: Pine cones, glitter and a hip-hop head for sale: red-hot artists reveal their Frieze stunners
articles.text:
First held in 2003, the Frieze art fair is a giant art supermarket that descends on Regent’s Park, London, every October. Some detest it for its blatant commercialism, others relish it as the opportunity to see a mind-boggling amount of contemporary art in one enormous tent. Here, eight British-based artists of the moment talk through what they’re showing.

How would you describe what you do?

I make sculpture. I work a lot with metal, fabrics, quite a collection of materials to make landscapes of figures that grow intuitively.

What’s the highlight of your career so far?

My exhibition at Hepworth Wakefield – getting major support in such an incredible institution.

Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.

Dead: Marisa Merz or Paul Thek. Both had an attitude of freedom of making. Living: Liliane Lijn or Donna Huddleston, who I know quite well. I love them and I think they’re amazing.

Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with.

I call them gesture works. They’re wall-based, but they allude to a crowd. They’re cast in aluminium and bronze and one of them has a piece of fabric.

Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?

Oh God, I can’t imagine. Hopefully still alive and excited with what I’m making.

How would you describe what you do?

I’m a figurative painter, but I also work across sculpture and installation. I’m self-taught, so my work has been described as outsider art. I’ll make work drawn from nursery rhymes and ethnographic texts.

What made you want to become an artist?

My mum came to the UK in the 80s from rural Bangladesh and we lived in a series of dilapidated houses. She was a textile worker so she made curtains for the house. My sister would salvage wood and make furniture, so I was immersed in organic homemaking.

What’s the highlight of your career so far?

Going to the Venice Biennale earlier this year. In light of the death of Koyo [Kouoh, who died while curating the show in which Rahman participated], the artists really came together.

Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.

Maybe it’s a cliche, but I really like Frida Kahlo. I think she did what I’m trying to do in the sense of hitting a balance between social realism, being political, speaking to the current social conditions and introducing a world of fantasy and mythology and dreams. And I really like the work of Toyin Ojih Odutola who had the Barbican Curve commission in London a few years ago. The storytelling and world building of that show was amazing. It’s a guiding star in terms of the direction I want to take my practice.

Tell me about the sculpture we’ve photographed you with. At Frieze in 2023, I was amazed by all these beautiful wooden shipping crates that were coming in like a big parade. I thought: these would be so beautiful if they were painted. This was designed as a seat and storage for my gallery team – it’s like set design. The fish pictures are drawn from kheta stitching, a folk craft in rural Bangladesh.

How would you describe what you do? I make paintings and I draw, mostly in charcoal. I look at figures in the landscape at liminal times. The figures are anthropomorphic, but they also are genderless. So there’s this queer undertone.

What’s the highlight of your career so far?

The Studio Voltaire show in London included the biggest painting I’ve ever made.

Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.

I love Turner’s abstraction of the landscape, and his use of colour really inspired me when I was younger. His watercolours are so transcendent and he’s a master at capturing atmosphere. And I really love Nan Goldin. In a day when art is so capitalist and based on consumption, the artists who stand out are ones who are trying to bring about social change.

Tell me about the picture we’ve photographed you with.

It’s a large charcoal drawing of two figures following one another in a forest scene. The figures look quite adolescent, so it feels almost like an old film still. There’s something quite nostalgic about it.

Who would you like to buy it?

I would love someone who I really admire to buy it. I’m such a big fan of Anohni, but I doubt she’s going to buy my drawing.

Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.

It’s a head portrait. Portraiture has been such an incredible genre in painting, from the Mona Lisa to Girl with a Pearl Earring to Picasso’s The Weeping Woman. I’ve always wanted to deal with this genre in a way that felt unique to how I would understand it. I grew up in a very hip-hop culture and so I’ve been exploring how to make hip-hop versions of heads.

What do you hope will happen when it gets sold at Frieze?

Hopefully somebody would love to live with it. Because I think art should be lived with, whether that’s in a museum or someone’s house.

Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.

Tupac and Tupac. He’s the greatest artist in my lifetime. You’re born, there’s a trillion things to notice, and an artist is just someone who goes: “This thing has happened. This is how I feel about it. I’m going to make something that’s so convincing”, whether it’s a painting or a song or a dance performance or a lecture like Joseph Beuys used to do. And then all of a sudden you go: “I get that. That makes sense to me.”

Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years’ time?

I have four chapters in my life. The first chapter is called Garvey: Birth. I think you’re born twice. You’re born first physically, but then you’re born culturally. And culture tells you how to understand yourself, who to love, who to hate. It’s the value of things. The second chapter is called Malcolm X: Innovation, someone who completely reinvented himself and chose his identity. And then the third chapter is Audre Lorde: Power – a poet and writer and also from Grenada, the island my mom is from. And then the last chapter is called Biggie Smalls: Death.

How would you describe your work?

I paint to capture the vibrating luminous residue of a glance turning a fleeting sensory encounter into an enduring act of devotion.

What has been the highlight of your career so far?

Probably a major show that began at the Hepworth Wakefield in 2024. It toured to Graz in Austria and then it went to Museum Villa Stuck in Munich, so that was a really nice year for me because I got to follow the works around Europe and see them in different institutional contexts.

Name two favourite artists, one dead and one living.

I like Rudolf Stingel. Every show that I’ve seen of his is completely different. He’s very willing to take risks. And for a historical one, Piero della Francesca. I just love those Italian fresco panel paintings. His depictions of women are just glorious.

Tell me about the painting we’ve photographed you with.

It’s the first time that I’ve fused two quite disparate series of mine. It’s a face projected on to this sparkly glitter curtain and the painting’s called Cathexis, which is from a Greek word which means to invest your energy into a specific thing. There have been so many examples throughout history where humans have invested in transient materials such as silk or flesh or marble, materialisations of desire, so that’s what I’m trying to do in this painting. It speaks to my interest in drapery and hair and in female beauty.

What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?

Oh, that’s a hard question. Well, I put a lot of trust in my gallery with placing it with someone who has a knowledge of my work, supports my practice and would loan it to some museum shows maybe later down the line.

What would you say the highlight of your career so far has been?

My show at Wolverhampton Art Gallery this year. I wanted to bring my work back to the city and to people who have varying understandings of art because of the degradation of the education system, and that was a privilege. To see them want to know more was highlight of my life. And I’ve got a solo show at South London Gallery coming up. I think I’m going to be the youngest person ever to do a solo show in that space. And that’s just like, Jesus Christ, how did we get here? I’m a kid from Wolves, you know what I mean? It’s all a bit mad.

Tell me about the paintings you’re showing at Frieze.

One’s called Gulliver’s Forrest and the other’s called Miss Mammy. They were made after the Wolverhampton show and before the beginnings of this new body of work. You’ve got periods of time where you can explore and mess around – that’s what it was.

What do you hope happens to this painting when it’s sold?

The most important thing is that the works are looked after and appreciated. So ultimately an institution [buying it] would be great but it needs to be somebody that will be responsible for it as my career grows, and not be flipping it.

Who are your two favourite artists, one dead and one living?

Rothko is my north star for what it means to make paintings. And alive, I think Ruprecht von Kaufmann is a phenomenal painter, and so is Andrew Cranston. I like bad-boy painters. In the pursuit of greatness you need to be reaching up to something.

Is it true that Stormzy has been coming by your studio?

Yeah, he came the other day. But ultimately, he’s just a guy who’s got interest in art and wants to see the work.

How would you describe your work?

I work with a combination of painting, printmaking and photography, all at a very intimate scale. The canvases are cut from materials more common for clothing and sometimes out of my own clothing. There’s often like a conceptual play between the textile subject and the surface, so if it’s made from a suede jacket, the work will depict the suede jacket. I’m interested in the way things like eBay might be the record of our culture in the future and what’s happening to this digital archive. But I’m also really interested in creating atmosphere and the qualities of light and how objects can suddenly express an inner emotion.

What’s been the highlight of your career so far?

I saw a big Paul Nash retrospective 10 years ago at Tate Britain and became a massive fan. There’s a particular painting of his, Dead Spring, at Pallant House [in Chichester] which I used to look at on my way to or from work when I was teaching. They recently acquired work of mine and in the summer I went to see it and it’s hung opposite Dead Spring. My own work has become part of that conversation in the gallery.

Can you name two favourite artists, one dead and one living?

Eileen Agar as my dead artist. I like that she just did her own thing for her whole lifetime, and I like her approach to materials and to collage. Francis Offman is my favourite artist at the moment. He’s using digital technology to fabricate these large weavings but then painting on them. The colours are amazing.

Tell me about the work you’re showing at Frieze.

It’s called Statues Also Die (Man Ray). It’s based on a photographic image I took of a Man Ray monograph covered in pine cones and forest-like debris during a residency at a museum in very rural Denmark 10 years ago. The title references the 1950s film by Alain Resnais and Chris Marker [and Ghislain Cloquet] which explores the shifting power of images according to different contexts and that’s something I’m interested in doing in my own work.

Who would you like to buy it, and who would you hate to buy it?

I enjoy making the work, but I don’t get overly attached to it once it leaves the studio. I feel like I let it go on its own journey, which I leave to other people.

How would you describe your work?

I came to the studio via a non-linear path. I studied science then had various jobs and set up a startup with my sister. Central to my practice is rejecting traditional materials and embracing imperfections. That’s informed by having to make art at home for a long time in cramped spaces.

What has been the highlight of your career so far?

My show at the South London Gallery was a turning point. The demographic wasn’t a sort of homogeneous room of art-world folk, politely nodding at the wall text. We had lots of local young people coming in, genuinely reacting to the energy of the work and the materials. It centred around this idea of roller-skating as a motif and some people turned up on their roller-skates.

Can you tell me two artists you love, one living and one dead?

Matisse had this ability to leave the rough in there as well as the polished, clean line. Chris Ofili has parallels with Matisse, and there’s something I always try and take from both of those artists.

Can you tell me about the picture that we’ve photographed you with?

That picture is called Game On (Crane’s Cut) and it’s on suede mat board, which forces a battle between painting and drawing because I have to use oil sticks and pastels and stuff. It shows a woman shuffling cards and it’s about the seductive but scary ideas of chance. It’s using that as a motif to explore the luck of global migration and the lottery of birth. I’m Ugandan, and there’s this crane flying across the picture, referencing the national bird of Uganda, the crested crane.

Where do you think you’ll be in 20 years?

My work has always been informed by not having much time – I’m currently pregnant with my third child. Time is such a luxury, isn’t it? I hope I have that space to explore other media, to make sculpture, to make an installation.

Frieze London runs from 14-18 October

articles.title: Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph
articles.text:
Fifteen centuries ago, the Byzantine archbishop Theophilus of Adana did first-hand business with the devil for his own superficial betterment. Today, we just blindly tick a little box marked “accept terms and conditions” or let high-street snake oil merchants inject poison into our faces. The Faustian pact has become as depressingly banal as it is endemic and destructive – and unlike Theophilus, we can’t rely on the Virgin Mary to save us now. In the midst of headlines about AI destroying humanity, the idea of listening to music submerged in precisely this shade of doom might sound like, well, hell. If anyone can thread that poisoned needle, it’s Fontaines DC.

When the Dublin band introduced their last album, 2024’s Romance, it came with a surprise new look. Their uncoordinated jeans and shirts had been replaced by neon hair, shiny trousers and bug-eyed sunglasses that split the difference between Korn and the Prodigy. As they faced up to having traded their anonymity to become arena fillers, it wasn’t hard to read this look as a sort of protective cosplay, a cybergoth Sasha Fierce for five fairly low-key Irish lads trying to make peace with leaving their roots behind. Newly melodic and lavishly produced, Romance made no bones about the band’s ambitions and became their first platinum-certified album.

For their fifth LP, Fontaines’ wardrobes are more or less back to normal as the music reaches new heights, indicating a level of comfort and confidence that resounds through their most formidable, cohesive record. Frontman Grian Chatten has said he wanted to write about the context collapse of social media and the willing degradation of what it means to be human, living in a time when “the mask is wearing the face a little more”. For all that might sound ripped from the headlines, Dopamine Chamber embodies the idea with poetry and a frankly thrilling and terrifying aptitude for seduction. Chatten’s lyrics repeatedly question reality and the truth that animates desire while at the same time offering promises of salvation that may or may not be what they seem. Yet the band’s darkly alluring music, full of heady absolution, makes it impossible not to succumb.

Lead single Marianne makes that intention explicit. “I can help you disappear,” Chatten chants over spiralling strings – glinting wormholes amid the pearlescent cosmic gloom. It is a massive song, a beckoning void. There are few more cringeworthy musical tropes than when bands pre-emptively scale up for stadiums without having the substance to scaffold it – making a meal out of crumbs – but Fontaines pull off that kind of ecstatic overwhelm again and again on Dopamine Chamber.

Ahead of the record, guitarist Conor Curley said he wanted to avoid sounds that immediately recalled historic bands. They don’t quite reinvent the wheel – Happy for You has the Cure’s unmistakably sour, lonely twang; Mimesis a roughshod New Order bassline; Demolition a sledgehammer grunge attack – yet they sound more like artefacts in the band’s gorgeous ruin of a soundworld than pastiche. Happy for You is full of beguiling flotsam, subtle echoes of pastoral guitar twang rippling like seaweed in the waves. You could spend a dozen listens focusing on the fine detail here – the agitated Tongue mixes Lankum’s dank chill with a taunting, pisky-like backing singer – but Dopamine Chamber gets its immediacy from Chatten’s scene-stealing vocal performances.

He swerves between indie rock’s best swoon since Morrissey and an insistent, addictive attack. One Man mixes both: “Do you have a genuine need to be desired / Call me up any time that you wanna fly yeah,” he incants against a wistful string crescendo, radiating both the possibility of redemption and the sense that accepting might mean grasping tight to Icarus’s feathers. At moments, Chatten’s voice hits on the level of pure sensation, feeling almost invasive in its capacity to worm its way into your veins: the way he exhales “I sweeeaaaaar” on Happy for You, or “surely you’ll wake up in yourself” on Mimesis.

Plus if you’re going to invite Rosalía to be the first guest on any Fontaines record, you’d better be able to hold your own. Channelling Morricone grandeur and mid-century balladry, the absolutely astonishing duet Where Is Gone? is as spellbinding as Nick Cave and PJ Harvey’s Henry Lee and a peerless would-be Bond theme that’s too good for the ailing franchise. The pair swirl around one another, beautiful and deadly as thick smoke.

articles.title: Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion
articles.text:
The British are perverse. We fetishise our failures, even if they are essentially tangential to a national narrative that should be about imperial conquest, slavery and being unremittingly unpleasant to foreigners. We tell and retell, for instance, the story of Captain Scott even though he died in Antarctica in 1912 after losing the race to reach the south pole first to the unacceptably Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Similarly, Christopher Nolan’s 2017 film Dunkirk typified the British tendency to snatch national glory from the jaws of defeat. And then there was the tragicomic disaster of the Charge of the Light Brigade during the 1853-56 Crimean war in which our boys raced to putatively glorious if stupid deaths. It’s as if, for us British, pointless sacrifice and embracing failure are what heroism means. And our cinema has colluded with this perversity.

But there is an exception to this national veneration of failure. Britain has been reluctant to embrace its revolutionary defeats. There is, for instance, no film dealing with the Chartist movement’s 19th-century struggle for universal suffrage. Even more strikingly yet, it is only now, in 2026, that a film has been made about the calamitous 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, even though it is a pivotal event in British history. Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield as a – let’s just get this over with – revolting peasant, joins a mere handful of other movies, including Kevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo’s 1975 Winstanley, Bill Douglas’s 1986 Comrades and Mike Leigh’s 2018 Peterloo, that dare depict how radical collective action was crushed by a ruthless state.

For Stephanie Barczewski, author of Heroic Failure and the British, our fetishisation of glorious disaster is a corollary of the 19th-century British private school ethos of stoic duty and crypto-S&M suffering culled from an ancient Roman exemplar. Revolutionary failure doesn’t fit this template; hence, one might suppose, its absence from our cinema.

The Uprising, however, for all its flaws and missteps, is a bold attempt to correct a national wrong by depicting a collective uprising devoid of heroism. Greengrass tries to make sense of how a mass movement of riff-raff from the rough ends of Kent and Essex arose, and how its momentum was compromised of factionalism and conflicting aims. It shows how, ultimately, the revolutionary leaders were duped by the boy king Richard II, leaving the rebels winding up to be either slaughtered en masse in London’s Smithfield or skulking defeated back to their homes to work harder to pay the poll tax whose unfairness they had risen up against in the first place.

It is an important – if belated, improbable and commercially dubious – addition to our national story.

In contrast, other countries have been more fortunate in their revolutionary heritage and as a result their national cinemas teem with examples of successful uprisings. From the advent of cinema, for instance, Americans have incessantly revelled in making movies about their war of independence – including silent features such as 1917’s The Spirit of 76 and DW Griffith’s America (1924), not to mention Bugs Bunny in Friz Freleng’s delightful period romp of a cartoon Bunker Hill Bunny (1950). The French have been making cinematic homages to their 1789 revolution going back the 1913 biopic Robespierre.

In Russia, Grigori Aleksandrov and Sergei Eisenstein’s October, in 1928, typified how the Bolshevik revolution’s success against the odds made Russian spirit what it is. Movies such as Neil Jordan’s Liam Neeson-fronted biopic Michael Collins (1996) and The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006), set during the Irish war of independence and starring Cillian Murphy, depicted the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage – even if the latter had an English director in the shape of Ken Loach.

But it isn’t just the deeply classist notion of what failures count as heroic that has made British cinema reluctant to embrace our failed revolutionary heritage. It is the result of how our culture has been reverse-colonised by Hollywood, with historical narratives only deemed filmable if they fit into American movie industry’s tropes. Whenever Hollywood deigns to make a movie about British history, it includes Downton-style upstairs-downstairs hokum, those crazy sexed-up murderous Tudors and, of course, that cod-historical franchise that never stops giving, Robin Hood.

Equally, it is axiomatic in Hollywood that political struggles are always about one thing – a very American notion of freedom, individual freedom from presumed oppression. That’s why Mel Gibson’s 1995 Braveheart was possible: even though William Wallace’s struggles against the English ended in failure with his execution at Smithfield (not far from where Wat Tyler was murdered by Richard II’s lackeys), the biopic involved the classic Hollywood trope of the little guy fighting for freedom. Any other political goal (tax reform, wealth redistribution, solidarity, fraternity) scarcely makes a dent in the Hollywood narrative juggernaut.

And that’s what makes Greengrass’s The Uprising problematic. Compromised by Hollywood values, it is conflicted about representing a failed political revolution as what it was – a collective struggle. It depicts the Peasants’ Revolt in the frame of one fictional man, Garfield’s Ploughman. Conceived by Greengrass as a representative everyman, Ploughman – with a disregard for historical truth that should make the film’s historical adviser Dan Jones wince – pops up Zelig-like to parlay with the king, catch the king’s mother’s eye, rally the rebels, scythe down the bad guys, as if he were a real-life historical figure. The collective struggle becomes individualised drama, betraying the positioning of the apostrophe – what happened in 1381 was the Peasants’ Revolt not the Peasant’s Revolt.

Worse yet, the film includes a very silly coda in which, a year after the defeat of the revolt, Ploughman and a rump of rebels have retreated to the English greenwood to form an outlaw band of unmerry men. The corollary of this coda is to make the Peasants’ Revolt a kind of origin story for the legend of Robin Hood, even though that is nonsense: the folkloric rebel operated – if at all – about 200 years earlier. The whole idea may seem ridiculous, but the US distributors for The Uprising, Focus Features, leaned into this barmy interpretation by changing the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood earlier this year, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”. Sensible Guardian readers will know of course that Robin Hood was a supporter of Richard I and foe of King John both of whom ruled England almost exactly two centuries earlier.

Such absurdities are a great shame since Greengrass’s – worthwhile – intention was to make a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that resonates topically for our age. A collapse in trust of our rulers, a seemingly endless cost of living crisis, widening inequality, political discourse dominated by lies and nonsense: 2026 is more like 1381 than we realise.

It’s worth pointing out that there has been one successful military revolution in British history, namely the English civil war. Cinema of course has been a failure at depicting it: there was Ken Hughes’s wildly inaccurate 1970 drama Cromwell starring Richard Harris and Alec Guinness and Mike Barker’s 2003 To Kill a King with Tim Roth and Dougray Scott. But our most enduring and successful revolution was scarcely cinematic: the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 in which the Catholic King James II was replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William III of Orange was hailed by Bertrand Russell as “the most moderate and successful of all revolutions. Its aims were modest, but they were exactly achieved.” Yawn! Who wants to see that movie?

Perhaps the greatest film about British revolutionary failure was the aforementioned Winstanley, about a group of proto-communists called the Diggers who settled common land on St Georges’s Hill outside Weybridge, Surrey during the English civil war. They hoped to create a utopia devoid of private property and for a few weeks lived self-sufficiently until they were violently evicted by the local gentry. To clinch the point that the Diggers’ experiment was a failure, just go on to property website Rightmove. There you can find a “stunning and elegant” £25m mansion on Cavendish Road, St George’s Hill with “fairway views, seven individually themed bathrooms, two staff apartments, and a leisure complex” and 1.5 acres of carefully landscaped gardens. Not what their leader Gerrard Winstanley wanted at all. He wrote: “Was the Earth made to preserve a few covetous, proud men to live at ease, and for them to bag and barn up the treasures of the Earth from others, that these may beg or starve in a fruitful land; or was it made to preserve all her children?” Our radical history, so often absent from our national cinema, has been built over in a field in Surrey for real estate scarcely any of us can afford. A very British coup if ever there was one.
